title: Pda

jokes.text: Darryl reads a sympathy card that says 'Congratulations, Darryl. Let's get wasted.'
jokes.setup: Someone (Michael) has gathered coworkers to give Darryl a card because his grandmother is near death. The gesture appears sincere and compassionate.
jokes.punchline: The card reads 'Congratulations, Darryl. Let's get wasted.' — the office thought it was his birthday.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional cold-open construction. The setup is genuinely sweet and misdirects the audience into a solemn register, then the punchline demolishes it perfectly. The joke reveals deep character truth about the office's obliviousness while also being structurally tight. The contrast between 'near death' and 'let's get wasted' is maximum comedic distance. Scores 8+ because it's a textbook great cold open that works on multiple levels.

jokes.text: More card messages are read aloud: 'Have fun today, big guy,' 'Oh yeah, party time, whoop-whoop,' 'Hooray, live it up big D,' 'Time to celebrate. You deserve this.'
jokes.setup: One misguided 'congratulations' card message was already the joke.
jokes.punchline: Multiple people signed with equally celebratory, party-themed messages, revealing the entire office thought this was a birthday card.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of multiple messages compounds the original joke effectively. Each new message adds to the pile-on absurdity. 'Whoop-whoop' and 'live it up big D' are funny in their specificity of enthusiastic obliviousness. Works as escalation of the cold open's premise.

jokes.text: Michael delivers 'birthday punches' to Darryl — 'One, two, three...' through '25' — while apologizing repeatedly
jokes.setup: Michael already humiliated Darryl with the wrong card. The situation couldn't get worse.
jokes.punchline: Michael doubles down by giving Darryl birthday punches, counting all the way to 25, saying 'I'm so sorry' mid-punch but not stopping.
jokes.explanation: Deeply character-specific to Michael: he recognizes he's causing harm but can't stop himself from committing to the bit. The apology mid-punch is what elevates this — the acknowledgment that he knows it's wrong but presses on anyway is quintessential Michael Scott behavior. The sheer count to 25 is the sustained cringe payoff.

jokes.text: Birthday punches — someone off-screen begins counting birthday punches as a 'joke' while Michael apologizes
jokes.setup: The card situation has already been mortifying; the scene should end
jokes.punchline: Someone begins delivering birthday punches and counts all the way up past 20, as Michael apologizes helplessly
jokes.explanation: Competent escalation of the birthday mix-up gag. The joke is that whoever is delivering punches hasn't gotten the memo and just keeps going. Michael's repeated apologies while the counting continues is good cringe. Slightly broad but lands as a satisfying capper to the cold open sequence.

jokes.text: Andy advises Darryl to order a cheeseburger at Blu Wasabi: 'They say they won't do it, but they will if you make a scene.'
jokes.setup: Darryl is excitedly telling the office about his Valentine's Day date at a sushi restaurant.
jokes.punchline: Andy's advice is to cause a scene at a high-end Japanese restaurant to get a cheeseburger — delivered as if this is wisdom.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly calibrated Andy Bernard joke — entitled, oblivious, confidently dispensing terrible social advice as if it's helpful. The specificity ('they say they won't do it, but they will if you make a scene') is what makes it land. Highly quotable and character-specific.

jokes.text: Michael and Holly's extended goodbye: 'Okay, bye. Okay, bye. (both moan) I'll miss you. Miss you. Okay. I'll be in my office if you need me. Bye-bye. (kissing) Bye. Okay, bye. Bye. Bye. Okay. One more big one. Don't go. I don't want you to go. Let go. Don't go.'
jokes.setup: Michael is merely walking from one part of the office to his own office — a distance of about 20 feet.
jokes.punchline: The goodbye is operatic and endless, complete with moaning, kissing sounds, and mutual pleading, for a separation of seconds.
jokes.explanation: A solid sustained cringe bit that establishes the episode's central comedic problem. Works because it's absurdly disproportionate to the situation (going 20 feet away). Slightly bloated by duration but the 'let go / don't go' escalation lands well.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'Everything you want in life, you get. And you can't work for it. It just comes to you.'
jokes.setup: Michael is reflecting on his relationship with Holly.
jokes.punchline: His 'wisdom' is the exact opposite of conventional motivational advice — a perfectly wrong life philosophy delivered with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael Scott false wisdom — the anti-motivational life lesson. Works because it's delivered with complete earnestness and is factually absurd. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Michael corrects Holly on 'scavenger hunt' vs 'treasure hunt': 'A scavenger hunt is where you find items from a master list. This is where you follow clues that lead to a prize. Common misuse. Good luck.'
jokes.setup: Michael has set up a romantic gesture for Holly and she calls it a 'scavenger hunt.'
jokes.punchline: Michael stops the romantic moment cold to pedantically correct the terminology, then dismisses her with 'Good luck.'
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: it's funny that Michael has this specific knowledge, and funnier still that he deploys it to kill the romantic mood of his own romantic gesture. 'Common misuse. Good luck.' is beautifully economical. Shows Michael's particular brand of getting in his own way.

jokes.text: Holly: 'But there's no clue.' Michael: 'Well, get to work.' Holly: 'I can't 'cause there's no clue.' Michael: 'The puzzle is the clue.'
jokes.setup: Michael has set up a treasure hunt but apparently failed to include a starting clue.
jokes.punchline: When Holly correctly identifies there's no clue, Michael doubles down with circular logic: 'The puzzle is the clue.'
jokes.explanation: Michael's confident nonsense — 'the puzzle is the clue' — is a good example of his pattern of making up an answer rather than admitting error. Quick, economical, and in character.

jokes.text: Oscar clears his throat loudly twice to get Michael's attention; Michael asks if Oscar is sick and if he needs to go home because he's 'grossing him out.'
jokes.setup: Oscar needs a signature from Michael and tries to get his attention diplomatically with throat-clearing.
jokes.punchline: Michael is oblivious to the social cue and instead interprets the throat-clearing as illness, complaining it's grossing him out — when the real gross behavior is Michael's PDA.
jokes.explanation: A functional joke built on Michael's obliviousness. The irony that Michael calls Oscar's polite throat-clearing gross while he's been making out in the office is solid but understated.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam laughing together at lunch, tip the waiter big, then Pam panics about losing her scarf — the camera cuts to them both laughing again at [03:22]
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are on a Valentine's Day lunch date, appearing happy and in sync.
jokes.punchline: The mundane panic about a lost scarf — the most minor possible crisis on a romantic date — is played with the same energy as a disaster, then immediately laughed off. Suggests champagne-fueled looseness.
jokes.explanation: A light visual/tonal beat showing Jim and Pam's easy chemistry. The scarf moment is slight and not particularly crafted, but the laughing cutaways do soft comedic work showing their contentment vs. Michael/Holly's chaos.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam's talking head about their Valentine's lunch: 'Never found that bottom, did we?' (re: bottomless champagne)
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam explain they did a Valentine's lunch to spend the night with their baby. They list the buffet amenities including bottomless champagne.
jokes.punchline: 'Never found that bottom, did we?' — delivered with cheerful smugness, implying they got very drunk at lunch.
jokes.explanation: A pleasant, well-delivered line that gets a mild laugh. The economy is good — 'never found that bottom' does efficient work suggesting pleasant day drinking. Not exceptional but competent.

jokes.text: Erin explaining she did Andy's sudoku by accident and is avoiding Stanley: 'I accidentally did his sudoku.'
jokes.setup: Erin and Andy are conspiring over Gabe's romantic treasure hunt clue.
jokes.punchline: The reason Erin needs to avoid Stanley is that she did his sudoku — a violation of office social protocol treated with the gravity of a federal crime.
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient joke that characterizes both Erin's haplessness and Stanley's terrifying territorial nature. The disproportionate fear of Stanley over a sudoku is funny and character-consistent.

jokes.text: Jim, visibly drunk from the lunch, flubbing a phone call: 'My name is (stammering) Jim Halpert, and I will fax it in to you... Under you. I'll fax it under you... Oh, excuse me. I just pissed my pants. Not really. I didn't really.'
jokes.setup: Jim is supposed to be working after a bottomless-champagne Valentine's lunch.
jokes.punchline: Jim is clearly drunk, fumbles basic professional communication, nearly says he pissed himself, then has to walk it back. The humiliation is compounded by his partial self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the Valentine's lunch setup works well. Jim Halpert being drunk at work is inherently funny because he's usually the competent straight man. 'I just pissed my pants. Not really. I didn't really.' is the highlight — the immediate overcorrection is a great comedic beat. High impact because the audience enjoys seeing Jim lose his cool composure.

jokes.text: Jim, still drunk, discovers a Valentine's card on his desk — reads it, realizes it wasn't meant for him, then tells the person 'I will not be your valentine. Oh, nuts.'
jokes.setup: Jim finds what appears to be a Valentine's card addressed to him and fills it out while on the phone.
jokes.punchline: He realizes it wasn't for him and flatly rejects the implicit sender: 'I will not be your valentine. Oh, nuts.' — all while visibly drunk.
jokes.explanation: A competent continuation of the drunk-Jim running gag. 'I will not be your valentine' as a firm rejection is funny given the context, and 'Oh, nuts' is a good button. Not exceptional but consistent.

jokes.text: The office group confessional about Michael and Holly's PDA culminates with Kevin saying 'I enjoy watching them because it makes me horny,' causing group disgust.
jokes.setup: Multiple employees are politely trying to express discomfort with Michael and Holly's PDA in a joint talking head, carefully couching their displeasure in supportive language.
jokes.punchline: Kevin, unaware of social filters, cuts through all the diplomatic hedging to announce he finds it arousing — triggering genuine disgust from the group.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character integration — only Kevin could say this. The joke works because the scene carefully builds diplomatic tension as everyone tries to stay polite, then Kevin obliterates the social contract entirely. The structure of contrasting the careful hedging ('obviously so happy for them both') against Kevin's unfiltered confession is well-engineered. The group's unified groan is the perfect button.

jokes.text: Andy describes his new girlfriend: 'She's neat. I met her at Darryl's cousin's party. We were the only two white people there.'
jokes.setup: Andy is asked to describe his new girlfriend.
jokes.punchline: His descriptor for the romantic connection is that they were 'the only two white people there' — an obliviously awkward racial observation delivered as if it's a charming meet-cute detail.
jokes.explanation: A well-deployed Andy joke — his oblivious privilege is on full display. The joke works because he clearly thinks this is endearing context rather than an awkward thing to say. Character-specific and economical.

jokes.text: Oscar's description of Michael's kissing: 'I hear them kissing all the time. It's this horrible plipping sound... it's like Chinese water torture. Just... (imitates kissing) Like it's coming from my own head.'
jokes.setup: Oscar is articulating the precise nature of his torment from Michael and Holly's PDA.
jokes.punchline: He's given it clinical thought — identified the sound ('plipping'), compared it to torture, and now it's colonized his mind. The sound effect he makes makes it visceral.
jokes.explanation: 'Plipping' is an inspired onomatopoeic invention. Oscar's precise, analytical approach to describing his misery is character-specific and the sound effect that follows is a great visual/audio comedy moment. 'Like it's coming from my own head' is the well-earned escalation.

jokes.text: Holly's talking head: 'He can put both his legs behind his head.'
jokes.setup: Holly is describing Michael's animal magnetism and sexuality in a talking head confessional.
jokes.punchline: After building Michael up as a 'jungle cat' who 'exudes sex,' the specific evidence she offers for his sexual prowess is the ability to put both legs behind his head — a gymnastic feat, not an erotic one.
jokes.explanation: The brevity and specificity are the joke. Delivered deadpan after romantic buildup ('jungle cat,' 'exudes sex'), the gymnastic non-sequitur lands hard. Maximum economy — four words deliver the entire punchline. The visual image of Michael Scott doing this is inherently funny.

jokes.text: Michael calls a meeting, announces 'Michael Scott, Dunder Mifflin' as if introducing himself to his own employees, says it's 'apropos' then corrects to 'apro-propriate'
jokes.setup: Michael opens what appears to be a formal HR-style meeting with his employees
jokes.punchline: He formally introduces himself to people who clearly know him, then stumbles into the non-word 'apro-propriate' as a hybrid of 'apropos' and 'appropriate'
jokes.explanation: The self-introduction to his own staff is a reliable Michael Scott character beat. 'Apro-propriate' is a nice malapropism — the kind of correction that makes things worse. Character-specific and economical.

jokes.text: Michael, noting Erin's absence from the HR meeting: 'Speaking of, Gabe, I don't see Erin at this meeting. I also don't see Andy.' — followed by the office's 'Ooh' and 'Boom! Face!'
jokes.setup: Gabe, Erin's boyfriend, is running an HR meeting. Michael has called the meeting ostensibly about PDA.
jokes.punchline: Michael uses the HR meeting to publicly imply Erin (Gabe's girlfriend) is off with Andy, humiliating Gabe in front of the whole office. Gabe tries to play it cool ('I get it. Andy's slamming my girlfriend. Very funny.') and fails.
jokes.explanation: Michael weaponizes the HR meeting immediately for petty drama. The office's collective 'Ooh' and 'Boom! Face!' is a great reaction beat. Gabe's attempt at a breezy 'I get it, Andy's slamming my girlfriend' while clearly mortified is excellent cringe. Good character dynamics at play.

jokes.text: Gabe uses Jim and Pam as the example of acceptable office romance: 'They don't touch. They don't kiss. You would hardly even know they were husband and wife.'
jokes.setup: Gabe is presenting his anti-PDA policy and needs a positive example of appropriate workplace romance.
jokes.punchline: He holds up Jim and Pam as the gold standard — praising them for being so repressed that their marriage is invisible. Jim and Pam's pleased reactions ('Did it. Yeah! Love it.') add another layer.
jokes.explanation: A good ironic inversion — the 'compliment' is actually that their marriage is invisible. Jim and Pam pumping their fists ('Did it!') at being complimented for not seeming married is a funny reaction beat that works on its own.

jokes.text: Dwight adds 'booby honking' and 'butt honking' to the list of prohibited PDA behaviors. Gabe confirms: 'All the honkings.'
jokes.setup: Gabe is listing prohibited PDA behaviors in a formal HR meeting.
jokes.punchline: Dwight volunteers 'booby honking' and 'butt honking' as specific behaviors, and Gabe solemnly ratifies 'all the honkings.'
jokes.explanation: Dwight's contribution to an HR policy meeting is perfectly in character — he takes the task seriously and escalates it with his own violent/absurd additions. Gabe's bureaucratic 'all the honkings' is a great straight-man button. 'The one where you start in a crouched position, then you leap...' being cut off before it completes adds another layer.

jokes.text: Dwight begins describing a PDA behavior: 'The one where you start in a crouched position, then you leap...' — cut off before completion.
jokes.setup: The office is listing prohibited PDA behaviors in the meeting.
jokes.punchline: Dwight begins describing an elaborate, physically acrobatic sex move — we never hear the end but the imagination fills in something horrifying. Gabe cuts him off with 'you know it when you see it.'
jokes.explanation: The interrupted description is funnier than any completed version could be — a textbook example of comedy of implication. The crouching starting position alone is a rich comedic image. Deeply Dwight-specific: only he would know this move, have done it, and feel comfortable mentioning it in an HR meeting. The economy of leaving it unfinished is masterful.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Whispering and tickling have their place in business.'
jokes.setup: The office is listing the PDA behaviors Michael commits — flirtatious whispering, flirtatious tickling.
jokes.punchline: Michael defends these behaviors as legitimate business practices.
jokes.explanation: Eight words, high quotability, perfect economy. Only Michael Scott would argue that tickling has a place in business. The brevity and confidence of the delivery is what makes this work.

jokes.text: Michael: 'That thing where you softly exhale on her neck.' Pam lists it as PDA. Michael: 'Okay, yeah, that's pretty hot. I will give you that.'
jokes.setup: Pam lists Michael's PDA behaviors including neck-exhaling.
jokes.punchline: Michael momentarily snaps out of his denial to sincerely agree that neck-exhaling is 'pretty hot' — breaking his own argument mid-stream.
jokes.explanation: Michael's inability to maintain his own defense when confronted with something he genuinely enjoys is a good character beat. 'I will give you that' as a concession mid-argument is charming and character-specific.

jokes.text: Dwight's confession: 'I have had intercourse in the office.' Then lists others: 'As has Angela. As has Ryan. As has Kelly. As has Meredith. As has Phyllis. As has Darryl. As has Creed. As has Michael. As has Holly.'
jokes.setup: Michael argues that everyone is a hypocrite about PDA. He calls for a confession.
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately and matter-of-factly discloses his own intercourse in the office, then names nearly the entire office roster — each name getting a bigger laugh as the list grows.
jokes.explanation: The accelerating list structure is a classic comedy engine and well-executed here. Dwight's unblinking matter-of-fact delivery of workplace sex confessions, naming Creed and Darryl as equal participants, is funny at each beat. The structure (confession → list → escalation) is strong. Each new name adds surprise value.

jokes.text: Dwight adds Kevin to the list. Office: 'With who?' Kevin: 'She goes to another school.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has listed nearly every office member who has had sex in the office. Kevin is added last.
jokes.punchline: 'She goes to another school' — the classic excuse for a girlfriend nobody has seen, delivered by Kevin with complete seriousness.
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode. The setup is perfectly constructed: Kevin being the last name on the list creates an expectation that he's merely another entry, then 'With who?' shifts the premise, and Kevin's 'She goes to another school' is a brilliantly economical punchline that works on three levels simultaneously: it's a playground excuse for a nonexistent girlfriend, it reveals Kevin's arrested development, and it retroactively casts doubt on everything. Maximum economy, perfect character integration, genuinely quotable and rewatch-worthy. This is the kind of joke that gets clipped and shared.

jokes.text: Michael proposes designating office closets as 'hook-up zones': 'One for each base, no homers.' Dwight immediately asks: 'What is the hook-up zone policy on masturbation?'
jokes.setup: Michael is proposing a solution to the PDA problem: designated hook-up closets.
jokes.punchline: The proposal immediately generates a logical edge-case question from Dwight — the masturbation policy — which Michael answers with 'Pro.'
jokes.explanation: Dwight treating the hook-up zone as a policy question requiring clarification on edge cases is deeply character-specific — he always finds the procedural angle. 'Pro' as Michael's one-word answer is perfectly economical and shows Michael's genuine enthusiasm for solving this 'problem.' The whole sequence (three closets, one for each base, no homers) is absurdist management comedy at its best.

jokes.text: Oscar: 'I love working at Dunder Mifflin, a division of Taliban enterprises. That's weird. I mean, that's weird to have sex in the office.'
jokes.setup: Michael has just proposed a policy allowing sex in designated office closets.
jokes.punchline: Oscar's withering 'Taliban enterprises' comparison followed by his meta-correction ('That's weird') is a sign of how far the meeting has gone.
jokes.explanation: The Taliban comparison is a bit of an odd choice that doesn't quite land cleanly, but Oscar's incredulous witness to the proceedings is consistent characterization. The self-correction ('That's weird... I mean, that's weird') is a nice touch of his articulate discomfort.

jokes.text: Erin and Andy's whispering scene in Darryl's office — whispering about whether Darryl can hear them, then testing by calling him a jerk, then immediately apologizing.
jokes.setup: Erin and Andy are trying to investigate Gabe's treasure hunt clue in Darryl's office without disturbing him.
jokes.punchline: They debate in whispers whether Darryl can hear them ('I feel like I'd be able to hear us at this level'), then test it by calling him a jerk, then when Darryl confirms he can hear, Erin immediately shushes Andy and says 'no more talking.'
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed escalating awkwardness beat. The logic of 'I think it's okay' → 'let me test by insulting him' → immediate mortification when confirmed he can hear is both absurd and character-true for Erin. Darryl's patient 'I can hear you' is a perfect straight-man line.

jokes.text: Gabe's treasure hunt song plays on a boom box: '(Singing) The temp at night / The temp at night'
jokes.setup: Gabe has set up a romantic Valentine's Day treasure hunt for Erin, and the next clue is a song on a boom box.
jokes.punchline: The romantic song is about 'the temp at night' — Gabe's loving nickname for Ryan is completely bizarre as a romantic lyric, suggesting Gabe put serious creative effort into something deeply, profoundly uncool.
jokes.explanation: Gabe's treasure hunt reveals his particular brand of romantic ineptitude — not just uncool, but specifically referencing office temps in his love songs. The fact that he thought this was romantic is the layered joke. 'The temp at night' is an inherently funny phrase as a song lyric, with Andy's baffled 'Temp at night? What do you...' adding a great reaction beat.

jokes.text: Andy and Erin struggle to decode the treasure hunt instruction 'pick it up, take it out' — repeating it back and forth in confusion.
jokes.setup: Gabe's treasure hunt song has a line about 'pick it up, take it out' as a clue.
jokes.punchline: Andy and Erin, both somewhat dim, struggle to parse the instruction, repeating it back and forth as if that will help: 'Pick it up. Take it out. Pick it up.' This goes on much longer than necessary.
jokes.explanation: This bit runs slightly long. The confusion is character-true for both Erin and Andy but the joke doesn't build to much — it's sustained mutual incomprehension without a strong payoff. Competent but the economy score suffers.

jokes.text: Michael returns to the meeting room, claims he 'forgot to collect his things,' and Holly narrates: 'Ah, the old leave behind. Oldest trick in the book. Good thing it's working.'
jokes.setup: Michael has agreed to stop PDA in the office. He immediately returns under a pretense.
jokes.punchline: Holly sees through the 'leave behind' tactic instantly but is charmed by it anyway — 'Good thing it's working' reveals she's a willing participant in Michael's transparent scheming.
jokes.explanation: A warm beat that shows why Michael and Holly work — she sees his moves clearly and is charmed anyway. 'Oldest trick in the book. Good thing it's working' is a nice double beat.

jokes.text: Michael explains why he sits on Holly's lap: 'I don't sit on your lap because it's comfortable. I sit on your lap because I like the way your thighs feel on my butt.'
jokes.setup: Holly suggests Michael stop PDA if it makes coworkers uncomfortable.
jokes.punchline: Michael clarifies the specific tactile reason he sits on her lap — it's not about comfort, it's about the sensation of her thighs on his butt. More information than anyone needed.
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael overshare — the clarification makes everything worse. The specificity of 'the way your thighs feel on my butt' is both TMI and somehow tender, which is the Michael/Holly dynamic in miniature. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'Holly and I are like Romeo and Juliet, and this office is like the dragon that kept them apart.'
jokes.setup: Michael is framing the office's objections to PDA in literary/dramatic terms.
jokes.punchline: His Romeo and Juliet metaphor breaks down immediately — there's no dragon in Romeo and Juliet. He's conflated two stories, delivered with complete certainty.
jokes.explanation: A great Michael Scott malapropism/myth confusion. He reaches for literary gravitas and lands in a completely different genre (dragon fantasy). The confidence of the delivery is key. Highly quotable — this line gets repeated. Strong character integration because his particular blend of cultural aspiration and ignorance is uniquely Michael.

jokes.text: Michael tells Holly he loves her. They negotiate what kind of love: 'Do you mean you love me like, Hey, there's Holly, I love that girl, or do you mean you love me like you love me love me?' — 'I love you love you.' — 'You love me love me.' — 'I love you love you.'
jokes.setup: Michael spontaneously tells Holly he loves her for the first time, one week into their relationship.
jokes.punchline: The negotiation of exactly which kind of love devolves into a charming recursive loop of 'love you love you / love me love me' that's both comedically absurd and genuinely sweet.
jokes.explanation: This works on multiple levels — it's genuinely comedic in its recursive absurdity (the negotiated 'love you love you') but also emotionally resonant, which is this episode's tonal peak. The audience is laughing and feeling something simultaneously. Elevated by Holly's specificity in parsing the exact kind of love being declared.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head after the love declaration: 'I am really disappointed in the office's policy on PDA at this moment.'
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly have just declared love for each other and clearly want to make out.
jokes.punchline: Michael can only express his frustration at not being able to kiss Holly by complaining about the office PDA policy — hilariously misplaced bureaucratic grievance at a deeply romantic moment.
jokes.explanation: A nice callback that finds Michael using the language of the HR meeting to express genuine romantic frustration. His complaint is formally worded ('the office's policy') at the most romantically charged moment of his week. Good economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'Yeah, whatever. No big deal. Just the hottest girl in the world loves me.'
jokes.setup: Michael has just had Holly declare love back to him.
jokes.punchline: His attempt at casual understatement ('yeah, whatever, no big deal') collapses immediately into the reveal of his actual feeling ('just the hottest girl in the world loves me') — the self-correction shows he cannot maintain the cool.
jokes.explanation: The three-beat structure (fake cool → collapse → genuine joy) is efficiently executed. Michael's inability to be genuinely cool even for a single sentence is character-true and endearing. Good economy.

jokes.text: Andy and Erin finding Ryan in the break room/office — it's implied he's with a woman. 'Oh. Cool.' followed by Andy and Erin gasping and looking away.
jokes.setup: The treasure hunt has led Andy and Erin to Ryan as a clue about 'the temp at night.'
jokes.punchline: Ryan is apparently in a compromising position (the audience sees the reaction — Ryan adjusting, Erin gasping 'Oh my God. Hanks'). The implication of what was happening is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A reliable implied-visual gag. The 'Oh. Cool.' from Andy is a great reaction beat. Erin's 'Oh my gosh. Hanks' is puzzling without video but clearly a reaction to something physical. Works but relies entirely on visual comedy we can only infer.

jokes.text: Ryan accuses them of wanting to have sex in his office. 'You wanted to have sex in my office.' Andy: 'No. Definitely not. That's disgusting.' Ryan: 'It's cool. Just um, try to put everything back where you found it. Text me when you're finished. I'll be out here.'
jokes.setup: Andy and Erin have stumbled into Ryan's office looking for the treasure hunt clue and interrupted him.
jokes.punchline: Ryan, completely unfazed, assumes they want to use his office for sex and accommodatingly offers to wait outside — normalizing something utterly bizarre as standard office procedure.
jokes.explanation: Ryan's blasé offering of his office for sex — 'Text me when you're finished. I'll be out here' — is perfect character comedy. It suggests this happens regularly or that Ryan finds it entirely unremarkable. The contrast between Andy's horrified denial and Ryan's casual accommodation is a great comedic juxtaposition.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam talking head — Jim: 'No, because the office isn't what I'd consider a romantic place.' Pam: 'Besides, we have something those other people don't have, which is a home and a bed. And a shower.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam clarify they have never had sex in the office.
jokes.punchline: Pam's list of what makes their situation superior — 'a home and a bed' — is punctuated by Jim adding 'And a shower,' which implies the other couples' encounters were distinctly unglamorous.
jokes.explanation: Jim's 'and a shower' is the best part — it implies the other couples' office encounters were somehow shower-adjacent without saying so. Good economy in that one added detail.

jokes.text: Michael and Holly try not to touch each other in the hallway — almost touching, pulling away, groaning, 'Almost got you. No, so close.' — worse than the PDA.
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly have agreed to stop PDA in the office.
jokes.punchline: Their attempt at restraint becomes a physical game of 'almost touching' that is more sexually charged and uncomfortable for observers than the actual PDA was.
jokes.explanation: A good visual/physical comedy bit where the 'solution' to the problem is worse than the problem. The concept is solid — abstinence theater being more provocative than the behavior — and the 'you're not touching me, I don't know what your body feels like 'cause I can't touch it' is a nice escalation.

jokes.text: Oscar's analysis of Michael and Holly's PDA, listing three possible causes including: '...you're at an age where your sexual climaxes aren't as powerful, so you need to overcompensate with foreplay, taboo behavior.' Michael: 'Yes, it was that. It's that one. Number three.'
jokes.setup: Oscar offers a clinical three-part diagnosis for Michael's excessive PDA behavior.
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately and enthusiastically selects option three — age-related sexual inadequacy — without hesitation, apparently preferring this explanation to the others.
jokes.explanation: Oscar's detached clinical diagnosis is well-crafted (three escalating options, including ecstasy and relationship urgency). But the punchline is Michael's instant enthusiastic acceptance of sexual inadequacy as the explanation — he finds it preferable to the alternatives. Great character beat.

jokes.text: Oscar admits: 'No one is a bigger fan of sexual touching than me. But with you two, it's reaching the level of a complex.'
jokes.setup: Oscar is explaining his objection to Michael and Holly's PDA.
jokes.punchline: Oscar establishes his pro-sex credentials before objecting, making his disgust more specific and funnier: he's not a prude, this is just actually too much.
jokes.explanation: Oscar's self-positioning as a sexual enthusiast who finds Michael's PDA excessive is a nice character beat — his gay identity adds an extra comedic layer to his credentials. 'Reaching the level of a complex' is a good clinical descriptor.

jokes.text: Michael approaches Holly: 'Give me all your money and take off your clothes.' Holly: 'We're not supposed to PDA.' Michael: 'Come on. Nobody's looking.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to be romantic/flirtatious under the new PDA restrictions
jokes.punchline: His attempt at flirtation sounds like a robbery, then he tries to get Holly to violate the PDA policy with 'nobody's looking'
jokes.explanation: 'Give me all your money and take off your clothes' as a romantic opener is a good Michael-ism. The fact that it sounds like a holdup is the joke. 'Nobody's looking' as the PDA workaround is a nice follow-up. Character-specific and economical.

jokes.text: In a tender moment where Holly is near tears about Nashua, Michael quietly says 'That's what she said.'
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly are having an emotional conversation about their relationship and the reality of long distance.
jokes.punchline: 'That's what she said' is deployed as a deflection from genuine emotion — Michael's reflex humor used to cope with vulnerability. Holly laughs softly instead of crying.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's finest comedic moment and one of the series' best uses of a running gag. The line is earned through years of setup (the running gag), and here it does triple duty: (1) it's technically a 'that's what she said' setup ('I'm not saying it won't be hard, but we can make it work'), (2) it breaks the emotional tension with Michael's signature coping mechanism, and (3) Holly's soft laugh rather than eye-roll shows she understands and accepts him completely. The economy is perfect — three words do the work of a speech. This is how you retire a running gag with dignity.

jokes.text: Erin, acting as hunt guide, tells Andy to 'enjoy a mid-hunt break' and to look for 'a heart or some (bleep) in the break room when you're through.'
jokes.setup: Erin has been co-opted as a guide/actor in Gabe's treasure hunt and is delivering scripted lines.
jokes.punchline: The scripted romantic treasure hunt instruction breaks down mid-sentence into 'a heart or some (bleep)' — suggesting Gabe's directions were vague and Erin is improvising/giving up.
jokes.explanation: The bleeping of 'some (bleep)' suggests Erin either swore or lost the thread entirely. Good character work — Erin trying to be romantically helpful and giving up. The flat delivery of 'some (bleep)' is funny.

jokes.text: Kevin looking through the window making faces to cheer Michael up — Michael coaches him: 'Do a monkey face. Do a monkey face.' Kevin obliges with monkey sounds. 'Jump. Jump up and down.' 'Throw your poop. Hurl your feces.'
jokes.setup: Michael is upset about Holly's imminent return to Nashua. Kevin spots him through a window looking sad.
jokes.punchline: Kevin tries to cheer Michael up by making faces, escalating at Michael's direction from 'monkey face' to jumping to 'hurl your feces.' Kevin obliges all requests earnestly.
jokes.explanation: An escalating physical comedy sequence. 'Throw your poop. Hurl your feces.' is the peak — both the escalation and Michael giving two synonyms for the same instruction ('throw your poop' then explaining with 'hurl your feces'). Kevin's cheerful compliance is character-perfect.

jokes.text: Michael and Dwight conceptualize 'Boner Bomb' as a movie: 'starring Jason Statham, or we go against type with an Eisenberg or a Michael Cera. Saving the world has never been this hard.'
jokes.setup: Dwight refers to Michael's romantic urgency with Holly as a 'sexual time bomb' or 'boner bomb.'
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately starts pitching it as a movie concept, with a tagline and casting considerations — the specificity of 'Eisenberg or a Michael Cera' against type is the comedic peak.
jokes.explanation: Michael's instant pivot to movie-pitching mode is perfect character behavior — he can't sit in an emotion without turning it into entertainment. 'Saving the world has never been this hard' as the tagline is genuinely funny. 'Against type with an Eisenberg or a Michael Cera' shows surprising specificity from Michael and is the funniest casting note.

jokes.text: Andy asks Erin: 'B-9. Like benign tumor.' Erin corrects: 'Maybe it's just more like Be mine.'
jokes.setup: Andy and Erin find a bingo-style card as a treasure hunt clue, reading 'B-9.'
jokes.punchline: Andy's first instinct is 'benign tumor.' Erin's gentler, more romantic interpretation ('Be mine') demonstrates that even Erin is more romantically calibrated than Andy.
jokes.explanation: A clean wordplay joke that also does character work — Andy's go-to interpretation of 'B-9' being 'benign tumor' says everything about how his mind works. Good economy and the contrast with Erin's romantic correction is a nice reversal of their usual dynamic.

jokes.text: 'Have you talked to her about our feelings? Women really go for that crap.'
jokes.setup: Michael is despairing about Holly having to leave
jokes.punchline: Kevin offers relationship advice, but his phrasing — 'our feelings' instead of 'your feelings,' followed by 'women really go for that crap' — is simultaneously wrong and accidentally wise
jokes.explanation: 'Women really go for that crap' is a great Kevin line — it's both cynical and correct, and the word 'crap' for emotional vulnerability is perfectly Kevin. 'Our feelings' is also funny (possibly a slip, possibly Kevin including himself in Michael's relationship). The line punches above its weight for economy and character specificity.

jokes.text: Michael tries to break up with Holly on Valentine's Day mid-emotion: 'Holly, I love you so, so, so much. And I think that we need to break up. What? Actually, it's Valentine's Day. Shouldn't be doing this today. I'll talk to you tomorrow.'
jokes.setup: Michael is overwhelmed by the idea of Holly going back to Nashua.
jokes.punchline: He opens with a love declaration then immediately pivots to a breakup, then catches himself — it's Valentine's Day — and literally schedules the breakup for tomorrow.
jokes.explanation: Michael's emotional self-contradiction (love declaration → breakup → 'actually it's Valentine's Day → reschedule the breakup for tomorrow') is executed in rapid-fire succession and is very funny. The scheduling of the breakup for 'tomorrow' is the perfect button. Deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Andy and Erin stare at each other after reading 'the real treasure is your Valentine's kiss' — both realize they're supposed to kiss, neither moves
jokes.setup: Gabe's clue ends with 'the real treasure is your Valentine's kiss' — but it's Andy (not Gabe) reading this with Erin
jokes.punchline: The camera lingers on the two of them processing the instruction and the moment's impossible awkwardness — they're supposed to kiss for Gabe's romantic gesture
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed awkward silence. The structural irony — Gabe's romantic hunt leading to this moment with the guy who has feelings for his girlfriend — is rich. The absence of dialogue is the joke; the audience fills in everything the characters can't say. Strong mockumentary craft.

jokes.text: Michael announces Holly and he are moving in together, then immediately tells Oscar: 'Oscar, this must be tough for you watching this go down. You could not stand in the way of true love, my friend.' Oscar: 'Are you kidding? I wasn't trying to break you guys up.' Michael: 'Better luck next time, pal.'
jokes.setup: Michael announces he and Holly are moving in together.
jokes.punchline: Michael has constructed an entire narrative in which Oscar was the obstacle to his love — with zero evidence. Oscar's clarification ('I wasn't trying to break you guys up') is ignored entirely. 'Better luck next time, pal' is Michael declaring victory over a battle that never happened.
jokes.explanation: Michael's fantasy narrative — in which Oscar was the dragon-antagonist of his love story — is pure Michael Scott delusion. It callbacks to Oscar's complaints without Oscar ever having ill intent. 'Better luck next time, pal' is a great closing taunt to a battle that was entirely in Michael's head.

jokes.text: As Michael and Holly leave making out, Michael calls back: 'Suck it, Oscar. This must kill you.' Oscar: 'I just told them to do it.'
jokes.setup: The office has told Michael and Holly to kiss as they leave. Michael is now interpreting Oscar's blessing as further evidence of Oscar's jealous defeat.
jokes.punchline: Oscar, who literally just encouraged the kiss, has to explain that he is not defeated — he orchestrated the moment. Michael doesn't process this.
jokes.explanation: A good button on the Michael/Oscar fantasy rivalry. Oscar's weary 'I just told them to do it' is the perfect exasperated straight-man line. Functional callback payoff.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam's talking head — after saying they 'took a walk' (implying office sex). Jim: 'We took a walk.' Pam: 'We took a walk.' Both clearly lying.
jokes.setup: The episode has established Jim and Pam as the couple who virtuously don't have sex in the office. They're seen looking disheveled/guilty.
jokes.punchline: Both immediately insist 'We took a walk' — the synchronized denial, delivered with zero conviction, reveals they did exactly what they claimed they never do.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed callback payoff. The setup was Jim and Pam's smug certainty that they don't do this, paired with their 'home and a bed and a shower' superiority. The callback — both saying 'We took a walk' simultaneously in flat denial — is among the episode's best structural comedy beats. Maximum economy (five words, repeated for emphasis), and the rewatch value is high because the earlier talking head gains an entirely new dimension. Ranks just below the 'That's what she said' moment.

jokes.text: Dwight's perfect Valentine's Day talking head: 'My perfect Valentine's Day? I'm at home, three cell phones in front of me, fielding desperate calls from people who want to buy one of the 50 restaurant reservations I made over six months ago.'
jokes.setup: Characters describe their ideal Valentine's Day.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's romantic fantasy involves scalping restaurant reservations — he has planned this months in advance, acquired 50 reservations, and finds the emotional satisfaction in others' desperation, not romance.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest character moments. Every element is Dwight-specific: the advance planning (six months), the scale (50 reservations), the multiple phones, the predatory pleasure in others' desperation. His 'perfect Valentine's Day' has nothing to do with romance and everything to do with commerce and dominance. This could not belong to any other character. Scores 8.5 because it's exceptional character comedy — comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor, with additional character specificity pushing it higher.

jokes.text: Dwight's second Valentine's Day beat: 'Anybody can be Prince Charming one day a year with the dinner and the flowers and all that. But you know what impresses me? When a guy can do that no days a year.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is continuing his Valentine's Day philosophy.
jokes.punchline: His romantic advice inverts the expected wisdom: instead of praising consistent romance, he praises complete romantic absence — 'no days a year.' Delivered with total conviction.
jokes.explanation: This is extraordinary character comedy writing. The structure is an inversion of a well-known sentiment ('one day a year vs. every day'), but Dwight's version goes further in the wrong direction: not 'no days' as lazy romanticism, but 'no days' as something that 'impresses' him — an actual romantic standard he aspires to. The construction is elegant ('one day a year... no days a year'), the delivery is deadpan, and it's deeply, specifically Dwight in a way no other character could deliver. Highly quotable. Comparable to and perhaps exceeding the 8.0 anchor example.

jokes.text: Contrast between Angela's Valentine's Day ('Flowers, diamonds, three-course meal, violinist comes to my table to serenade me') and Pam's ('Pizza, soda, the moon, someone to share it with').
jokes.setup: Characters describe their ideal Valentine's Day in an intercutting talking head.
jokes.punchline: Angela's elaborate fantasy (violinists, diamonds) vs. Pam's simple contentment (pizza, soda, the moon). The contrast does character work — Angela's romanticism is performative and transactional; Pam's is genuine.
jokes.explanation: A functional character contrast bit. Angela's escalating demands (violinist!) vs. Pam's genuine simplicity works as a character-driven closing beat. The humor is gentle — more sweet than funny, but the Angela moment (violinist) has real laugh potential.

jokes.text: Jim's answer to Pam's 'What are our plans for tonight?' is the sound of a bed creaking — he makes the noise himself.
jokes.setup: Pam has described her ideal Valentine's Day as simple and romantic — pizza, soda, the moon.
jokes.punchline: Jim answers her question about plans by imitating a creaking bed — a sound effect that is both an answer and a callback to the episode's sexual chaos — delivered deadpan.
jokes.explanation: A perfect closing joke — maximum economy (zero words), callbacks to the episode's running theme, and lands as a button for Jim and Pam's story. Jim making the sound effect himself rather than describing it is the extra layer of commitment that makes it work. Ends the episode on a laugh.

jokes.text: Jim asks Pam 'What are our plans for tonight?' Pam: 'Um...' then imitates a creaking bed.
jokes.setup: The episode closes with couples sharing Valentine's plans; Jim asks Pam
jokes.punchline: Pam's response is a bed-creak sound effect — simultaneously domestic (a real bed, at home) and the callback to their 'We took a walk' disclaimer
jokes.explanation: A great closing button. Pam's sound-effect response is maximally economical — one noise does the work of a whole sentence and pays off the Jim-and-Pam arc of the episode. The bed-creak as the final gag is satisfying, funny, and contextually rich.

tmdb_overview: The staff grows increasingly uncomfortable with Michael and Holly's PDAs. Jim and Pam regret a champagne luncheon. Andy horns in on a romantic treasure hunt Gabe arranged for Erin.
